Says what a pin on the e-file stops (the pawn cannot capture) and what ends it (a piece on e7, e6 or e5), and checks that before releasing the pin
States Black's plan after the queen move (defend e4 with a developing move, castle, regain d5) and the cost: the engine still prefers White in every main line
Shows by counting attackers and defenders that 4...f6 does not defend e4 and the pawn falls with check
Names what changes when White declines on move three, with game counts from our Lichess sample as results, with the sample size stated

steps.text: **The question of this lesson.** In the Elephant Gambit Black gives up a pawn for activity. This lesson adds what lesson 1 did not cover: White's other fourth moves, Black's plan after the queen move, and what happens when White declines on move three. By the end you can say why one fourth move keeps an edge and why tempting defences fail. Marks: [V] checked here, [S] our archive, [I] inference, [H] hypothesis.

steps.title: Is the pawn pinned?

steps.text: **A pin ends when the line is blocked.** The pinned pawn can still step forward along the file but can no longer capture, so the knight on f3 is safe from it. The pin lasts only while nothing else stands between the queen and the king. A piece on e7, e6 or e5 releases it; whoever releases it must check the result first.

steps.text: **Why the queen move is different.** It does two jobs at once: it attacks the pawn on e4 and pins it, so Black cannot use the pawn to attack the knight on f3. The three knight moves each leave the pawn on d5 for the black queen to take. [I] The pin is what the other moves lack, which is why only this move keeps a clear edge in the engine's list.

steps.prompt: [H] The knight move to d4 was chosen in 1,543 of our Lichess games and White scored only 44% with it. Offer one reason why players choose it, and say how you would test your reason.

steps.text: **Black's plan after the queen move.** Black cannot attack the pinned knight, so the plan is to develop with threats: defend e4 with a piece, bring out the bishop, castle off the e-file, and take back the pawn on d5 when it costs nothing. [S] Lichess sample: the knight to f6 in 1,623 of 2,310 games, the queen to e7 in 184.

steps.text: **What the other third moves show.** A gambit is a bargain that depends on the opponent's reply. If White takes on d5 and finds the queen move, Black has a real fight; the quiet third moves give Black an ordinary game. [H] A player who meets quiet third moves more often than the main line gets little from main-line preparation alone. Look at your own games to see which it is.

**Test yourself.** Three unlabelled positions. In each, say first which pieces are loose, who attacks and defends the key square, and which move keeps material. Some come from the main line, some from lines you have only seen once.

steps.prompt: Teach-back: in a few sentences, explain to a beginner what the queen move does that the knight moves do not, what Black's plan is, and why 4...f6 does not work. Self-check afterwards: did you say when the pin works and when it ends, give an example a beginner could set up on a board, and name one mistake to avoid? The app grades nothing; compare with the recap.

steps.text: **Recap.** 1. The queen move attacks the pawn on e4 and pins it. 2. A pin ends when a piece stands behind the pawn. 3. Knight moves let the black queen take back d5. 4. Black's plan: defend e4, castle, regain the pawn. 5. Count attackers and defenders after every exchange. 6. The engine prefers White in every main line. 7. Quiet third moves give ordinary games.
